clinicalPearls: MEF2C encodes a MADS-box (MEF2) transcription factor essential for neuronal differentiation, migration and activity-dependent synapse regulation.
Disease arises from heterozygous intragenic variants or 5q14.3 microdeletions encompassing the gene; both produce haploinsufficiency.
Core features are severe to profound intellectual disability, absent or minimal speech and marked early hypotonia.
Epilepsy is frequent, with variable seizure types and onset commonly in infancy.
Stereotypic movements (including hand stereotypies), poor eye contact and autistic features produce a Rett-like phenotype.
Most affected children do not achieve independent walking, and feeding difficulty and constipation are common.
Neuroimaging may show mildly enlarged ventricles, abnormal periventricular white matter or a hypoplastic corpus callosum.
Larger contiguous 5q14.3 deletions may involve neighbouring genes and broaden the phenotype.
reference.pathophysiology: MEF2C at chromosome 5q14.3 encodes myocyte enhancer factor 2C, a MADS-box transcription factor that acts as a master regulator of activity-dependent neuronal development, directing neurogenesis, neuronal migration and dendritic morphology while restraining excitatory synapse number. The disorder results from heterozygous loss-of-function point variants or 5q14.3 microdeletions that remove or disrupt one MEF2C allele, producing haploinsufficiency; contiguous deletions extending beyond the gene may add features from adjacent loci. Reduced MEF2C dosage impairs the downstream transcriptional programmes (including targets such as BDNF and immediate-early genes) required for cortical network maturation, yielding severe neurodevelopmental impairment, epilepsy and a Rett-like clinical picture.
additionalInvestigations: MEF2C sequencing via targeted gene, panel or exome testing
MECP2, CDKL5 and FOXG1 testing if the Rett spectrum is considered
redFlags: Regression or loss of previously acquired skills
Feeding difficulty with aspiration or faltering growth
New focal neurological signs prompting repeat imaging
reference.prognosis: A lifelong severe neurodevelopmental disorder; most individuals remain non-verbal with limited mobility and need full daily support, although seizures may be partially controllable and survival into adulthood is possible.
pitfalls: Clinically indistinguishable from Rett syndrome, so negative MECP2 testing should prompt MEF2C and microarray analysis
Small intragenic variants missed by microarray require sequence-based testing
Attributing stereotypies to idiopathic autism without genetic workup
Assuming a normal microarray excludes the diagnosis when a point mutation is responsible
references: Clinical dysmorphology and neurogenetics reference texts
management: Antiseizure medication tailored to seizure type to control the frequently associated epilepsy
Early developmental intervention with physiotherapy and occupational therapy for hypotonia and motor delay
Speech and language therapy with augmentative and alternative communication for absent or minimal speech
Feeding and swallowing assessment with nutritional support, and gastrostomy where feeding difficulty is severe
Manage constipation with laxatives and provide behavioural support for autistic features and stereotypies
EEG and brain MRI to characterise seizures and structural change, with ongoing developmental monitoring
Genetic counselling, noting most cases are de novo, with confirmatory testing and recurrence-risk assessment
Coordinate multidisciplinary paediatric neurology, developmental and therapy support for lifelong care needs
